newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Analysts up Sweden CPI forecasts after change.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Analysts up Sweden CPI forecasts after change.

text.p: Sweden's official statistics bureau said on Tuesday it would revamp its method for calculating the consumer price index, prompting analysts to revise their inflation forecasts upward.
But most analysts said that in the longer term there would be no difference between the old and news systems.

Statistics Sweden said it would use a new method to calculate inflation beginning next month. At the same time it said the new method made the year-on-year rate of inflation in March zero instead of a fall of 0.4 percent.
The office said it would publish revised figures for January 1995 to March 1997 when it released April consumer price data on May 15 at 0715 GMT.
The statistics office declined to say how other figures would look after the revision.

Several analysts said they would move their forecasts higher, following the lead of the statistics office, but played down the importance of the adjustment to anything more than a facelift for the data.

"We will probably revise our inflation estimates for the year upward by about 0.3 percentage points but in the long run there should be no difference between the old and the new method," said Hagstromer & Qviberg economist Sven-Arne Svensson.

"It's basically just a cosmetic change," said Union Bank of Switzerland European economist Darren Williams. He said he would not change his monthly forecast for April but would move his 1997 figure to a rise of 0.1 percent from a fall of 0.3 percent.
"We're moving towards a slightly more accurate measure but we're probably not there yet," he added. "The harmonised European Union figures probably give a better indication of the real picture."
The statistics bureau said it changed its method because of the refinancing of long-term mortgages that had taken place after interest rates fell in 1996.
Last year Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, cut its key repurchase rates 25 times from 8.91 percent in January to its current level of 4.10 percent.
"The method used until now has undervalued household interest costs for the repayment of property loans," Statistics Sweden said in a statement.
"Fixed rates are above current rates so people have possibilities to refinance them," Statistics Sweden spokesman Gosta Guteland told Reuters.
"Our model covers this, but it does not cover the sum people have to pay banks for the refinancing. We are going back to a model we used three years ago, which we have found to be better," he said.
The statistics office would not say how other figures would look after the revision.

Several analysts pointed out that the revised data was bound to be closer to the inflationary target of the Swedish central bank, which sets two percent as a goal with a one percentage point variance in either direction.
The Riksbank said it was too early to say what the effects of the change would be.

"We won't know the story until May 15 when the revised CPI statistics are presented. We will publish a new inflation report in one month," Jonas Ahlander, head of the Riksbank's division for price analysis, told Reuters.
"Today I can not say anything about what conclusion we will draw in it," said Ahlander.
